Birds that decide the trip

Black-tailed Godwits in the Netherlands

The Netherlands carries a large share of the western European breeding population, and the wet meadows of Friesland are where they are managed for. Display flights run through April and May, and the birds are gone again by July.

When April and May, with the first birds back in late February

Where The Frisian Lakes and Meadow-Bird Country, The Biesbosch and the Great Rivers

Eurasian Spoonbills in the Netherlands

Spoonbills nest on the Wadden islands and feed on the flats at low water. The colonies were down to a few dozen pairs in the 1960s and have recovered since. They are here from March and mostly gone by September.

When March to September, easiest on a falling tide

Where The Wadden Islands, The Wadden Coast and Lauwersmeer

White-tailed Eagles in the Netherlands

The first Dutch pair bred at Oostvaardersplassen in 2006 and the species has spread to the Biesbosch and the river floodplains since. Winter is the easiest time to see one, when birds from further north add to the resident pairs.

When All year, with the best viewing from November to March

Where Flevoland and the Oostvaardersplassen, The Biesbosch and the Great Rivers

Barnacle Geese in the Netherlands

Hundreds of thousands of geese winter on Dutch grassland, and Barnacle Goose is the one that arrives in the tightest flocks. They come in from October, spread across the north and the delta, and leave again through March.

When October to March, at their peak in December and January

Where The Wadden Coast and Lauwersmeer, The Zeeland Delta

Bluethroats in the Netherlands

A reedbed bird that sings from an exposed perch early in the season and becomes hard to find once the reed is up. Lauwersmeer and the Biesbosch are both reliable, and the second half of April is the window.

When Mid April to May, and they sing at first light.

Where The Wadden Coast and Lauwersmeer, The Biesbosch and the Great Rivers

Red Knots in the Netherlands

Knot pass through the Wadden Sea in tens of thousands on their way between the Arctic and west Africa. They feed spread across the flats and pack together on high water roosts, which is when they are worth timing a visit for.

When August to October and again in May, on a rising tide

Where The Wadden Islands, The Wadden Coast and Lauwersmeer

Middle Spotted Woodpeckers in the Netherlands

A bird that was barely Dutch until the 1990s and now holds a good population in old oak on the Veluwe and in Limburg. It calls most in early spring, before the leaves make the canopy hard to work.

When February to April, when the calling is at its most persistent

Where The Veluwe, Limburg and the Southern Hills

Kentish Plovers in the Netherlands

A small, scarce breeder now largely confined to the shell banks and bare sand of the delta and the newly built islands. Numbers are low enough that the nesting areas are fenced, and the birds are watched from the edge.

When April to July, from the marked edge of a breeding area

Where The Zeeland Delta, Flevoland and the Oostvaardersplassen

When to Go

The Dutch birding year is set by migration, not by rain. Spring fills the meadows and reedbeds with breeding birds, autumn moves hundreds of thousands of waders through the Wadden Sea, and winter brings the geese.

Spring

March to June

Meadow birds display, reedbeds fill up, and the woods are in full song from before six in the morning.

Go for Breeding birds, long daylight and the best song of the year.

Trade off School holidays and the bulb fields fill the coast, and rooms cost the most in April and May.

Typical daily average
  • March: 4 to 13 °C / 39 to 55 °F
  • April: 7 to 17 °C / 45 to 63 °F
  • May: 10 to 20 °C / 50 to 68 °F
  • June: 13 to 22 °C / 55 to 72 °F

Autumn

July to October

Wader numbers build through the Wadden Sea, and the coast picks up whatever is moving south.

Go for Big counts on the tidal flats, and a real chance of a scarce migrant on the islands.

Trade off The song has stopped, so you identify birds on plumage and call instead.

Typical daily average
  • July: 13 to 22 °C / 55 to 72 °F
  • August: 13 to 22 °C / 55 to 72 °F
  • September: 11 to 19 °C / 52 to 66 °F
  • October: 8 to 15 °C / 46 to 59 °F

Winter

November to February

Geese cover the grassland in six figures and diving duck gather on the IJsselmeer.

Go for The biggest concentrations of birds in the Dutch year, and the cheapest rooms.

Trade off Eight hours of daylight, a lot of grey overcast, and a wind off the North Sea with nothing to slow it down.

Typical daily average
  • November: 4 to 9 °C / 39 to 48 °F
  • December: 2 to 7 °C / 36 to 45 °F
  • January: 1 to 6 °C / 34 to 43 °F
  • February: 1 to 6 °C / 34 to 43 °F

The Wadden Islands

Dune, saltmarsh and tidal flat, two to three hours from Amsterdam plus a ferry

Five inhabited islands sit along the top of the country, each reached by its own ferry. Texel is the easiest first visit and the others get quieter as you go east. The tide sets the day here, and high water pushes waders onto roosts you can watch from a hide.

  • Habitat: Five inhabited islands strung along the largest intertidal mudflat system in Europe. Each runs a dune belt and pine plantation on its North Sea side into saltmarsh, polder and grazed grassland on the Wadden shore, and the flats exposed at low tide feed birds in their millions. Texel adds the Slufter, a valley the tide still reaches through a gap in the dunes.
  • When: Good all year, and best in the breeding season and spring passage from April to early June, then again from August to early November. Reserve interiors close on 1 March and their paths reopen on 15 August, so guided excursions are the way in through the summer.
  • Getting there: Ferries run from Den Helder to Texel, from Harlingen to Vlieland and Terschelling, from Holwerd to Ameland and from Lauwersoog to Schiermonnikoog. Holwerd sits on the road out of Leeuwarden with 3 km more to the pier, and Harlingen and Den Helder both have trains. Every island runs on cycle tracks and dike roads, and most Texel reserves can be watched from those without going in.
  • Look for: Eurasian Spoonbill, Pied Avocet, Bar-tailed Godwit, Red Knot
  • National parks: Dunes of Texel National Park, Schiermonnikoog National Park
  • Stops:
    • : A shallow roadside pool on the east coast of Texel. Watch it from the car on the dike road, with terns and waders at close range.
    • : A reserve built for waders beside the Wagejot, with a hide over its pools and islands. Entry is free.
    • : Wet grassland and brackish pools inland of the same dike road. You can see the whole of it from the roadside.
    • : A valley where the sea breaks through the dunes and forms salt marsh. Marked paths lead out from the car park.
    • : The undeveloped eastern third of Terschelling, salt marsh and beach plain. Get there by bike or on foot.
    • : A freshwater lake with a hide, a short walk from the village. Visitors leave their cars on the mainland.
    • : A chain of shallow lakes behind the dunes. A marked cycle route runs to them from the village.
  • Visitor centres: Ecomare, Texel
  • Also covers: Ameland, De Boschplaat, Terschelling, De Kroon's Polders, Vlieland, De Slufter, Texel, Dijkmanshuizen, Texel, Dunes of Texel National Park, Ecomare, Texel, Schiermonnikoog National Park, Utopia, Texel, Wagejot, Texel, Westerplas, Schiermonnikoog
  • Also watch for: Harbour and grey seals haul out on the sandbanks and are visible from the boat trips that run from every island. Harbour seal pups arrive in June and July, grey seal pups from November into January.

The Wadden Coast and Lauwersmeer

Freshwater lake, reedbed and open coast, two hours from Amsterdam

Lauwersmeer was cut off from the sea in 1969 and became a national park of reed, open water and rough grazing. The reedbed singers are nesting from the middle of April, and the surrounding coast is where the mudflat birds go once the tide covers the flats.

  • Habitat: A freshwater lake of 9,100 ha. A dam closed it off from the Wadden Sea in 1969, and it now holds reedbed, wet grassland and open water where the tidal inlet used to be. Outside the sea dike, 19 km of grazed saltmarsh and mudflat run on into the Wadden from Zwarte Haan east to the Holwerd pier.
  • When: Good all year. Marsh birds sing from late April, waders pass through in May, and White-fronted, Barnacle and Brent Geese fill the polders from November.
  • Getting there: From Leeuwarden drive east, then turn north through Dokkum to Anjum and Lauwersoog. From Groningen a single road runs north-west to the same harbour.
  • Look for: Bluethroat, Montagu's Harrier, Common Crane, Eurasian Spoonbill
  • Parks and reserves: Lauwersmeer National Park, Waddenzee (Natura 2000 site and World Heritage)
  • Stops:
    • : Two viewpoints over mud and shallow water at the south end of Lauwersmeer, free and open. This is the best wader watching in the north.
    • : A free hide over grazed marsh on the Groningen side of Lauwersmeer, a short walk from the parking.
    • : Wet grassland inside the Wadden dike near Lauwersoog. Watch it from the road and the dike.
    • : Outer salt marsh west of Holwerd, walked out along the dike. It becomes a high tide roost when the flats cover.
  • Also covers: Bantpolder, Ezumakeeg, Harlingen, Jaap Deensgat, Lauwersmeer National Park, Lauwersoog, The Noarderleech, Waddenzee
  • Also watch for: Konik horses and Highland cattle graze the reserve and keep the grassland open, and roe deer are regular at the edges. Otter has returned to the waterways and is occasionally seen at first light.

Groningen and Drenthe

Heath, bog and old woodland, two hours from Amsterdam

The two northern provinces hold the country's driest heath and its oldest peat bog at Dwingelderveld. Old pine and oak carry the woodpeckers, the open heath churrs after dusk from late May, and the heather is at its best from late July into September.

  • Habitat: Drenthe is largely sandy ground carrying heathland and mixed forest, with more farmland and younger woods than the Veluwe. Dwingelderveld National Park holds the best of the heath, fen and mostly coniferous forest, and huge numbers of waders roost there in summer, mainly Black-tailed Godwit and Whimbrel. Outstanding peat moor reserves survive at Fochtelooerveen in the extreme northwest and Bargerveen in the southeast. Most of Groningen is arable field on clay with a few large lakes and some mature wood in the southeast, and Zuidlaardermeer carries wide reedbeds along its west and south shores above some of the province's best bird meadows.
  • When: Good all year. Black Woodpecker and Woodlark are on site in all twelve months.
  • Getting there: Zuidlaardermeer lies 10 km southeast of the city of Groningen, between Haren, Hoogezand and Zuidlaren. Dwingelderveld has a nature information centre near Ruinen. In the southern outskirts of the city the Hoornse Dijk cycle track crosses the Hoornse Meer pool on a bridge that is one of the easiest spots in the country for nesting Penduline Tit. Schildmeer has a raised hide at Vossenbult, and the Veenhuizerstukken pools near Stadskanaal have hides on either side of the N33 and N366 junction.
  • Look for: Black Woodpecker, Woodlark, European Nightjar, Red-backed Shrike
  • National parks: Drentsche Aa National Park, Dwingelderveld National Park, Drents-Friese Wold National Park
  • Stops:
    • Fochteloerveen : A raised bog straddling Friesland and Drenthe, with a viewing tower and free entry. The Common Crane that recolonised the Netherlands nest here.
    • Dwingelderveld : A national park of wet heath and pools, with marked walks from several car parks. European Nightjar call in June and Black Woodpecker work the pines.
    • De Onlanden : A flooded peat basin south of Groningen, free and open, with cycle paths and hides. Eurasian Bittern and Western Marsh Harrier breed here.
    • : Lake edge and reedbed with a hide. Reach it from the village of Zuidlaren.
  • Also covers: Assen, De Onlanden, Drents-Friese Wold National Park, Drentsche Aa National Park, Dwingelderveld National Park, Dwingeloo, Fochteloerveen, Groningen, Zuidlaardermeer
  • Also watch for: Red deer, badger and roe deer live across the heath and old woodland, and adders bask on the sandy tracks at Dwingelderveld from April to September. Sheep flocks still graze the heather by arrangement.

The Frisian Lakes and Meadow-Bird Country

Wet grassland and shallow lakes, ninety minutes from Amsterdam

Friesland holds the largest share of the country's breeding Black-tailed Godwit, a bird the Netherlands carries much of the world population of. The wet meadows are managed for them, and April and May are when the display flights are constant.

  • Habitat: Wet clay meadow and shallow lake between the IJsselmeer dike and Sneek, with reedbed at the water's edge and grazed grassland behind. The IJsselmeer shore at Makkumer Noordwaard and Workumerwaard shelves so gently that easterly wind exposes mudbanks.
  • When: Good all year. Ruff gather on passage in March and April, Spoonbill and Black Tern feed on the exposed mud in late summer, and White-fronted, Barnacle and Pink-footed Geese hold the meadows from October.
  • Getting there: The motorway crosses the Afsluitdijk to Kornwerderzand, and a minor road parallel to its southern side runs east to Makkum, Piaam and Gaast on the coastal dike. Workumerwaard lies north-west of Workum: turn west across the dike 2 km south of Doniaburen. Sneek is the town for the Brekken.
  • Look for: Black-tailed Godwit, Northern Lapwing, Ruff, Eurasian Oystercatcher
  • National park: De Alde Feanen National Park
  • Stops:
    • Skrok and Skrins : Two small reserves near Wommels, managed for breeding Black-tailed Godwit and Ruff. Each has a viewpoint.
    • : Wet grassland on the IJsselmeer shore south of Workum. Watch it from the dike.
    • : Shallow shore and reed on the same coast. A hide sits at the end of a short walk.
    • De Alde Feanen : A national park of fen, reed and open water. Enter by boat or from the visitor centre at Earnewald.
  • Also covers: De Alde Feanen National Park, Makkumer Noardwaard, Skrok and Skrins, Sneek, Workumerwaard
  • Also watch for: Otter has recovered across the Frisian waterways since reintroduction, and brown hares box in the open fields through March and April. Roe deer search the ditches between the wet meadows.

The Weerribben-Wieden and the Salland Ridge

Lowland peat marsh and dry heath ridge, ninety minutes from Amsterdam

Northwest Overijssel holds the largest lowland peat marsh in northwest Europe, cut through by canals and reached by boat from Giethoorn or Ossenzijl. Reed and open water carry the marsh birds from mid April. An hour east the land rises into the Salland ridge, dry heath and pine, which holds the last Black Grouse in the Netherlands on a lek that is watched rather than approached.

  • Habitat: Shallow lakes, peat cuttings, reedbed, wet meadow and carr woodland in the north-west corner of Overijssel. Weerribben is the well-vegetated marsh of the pair and De Wieden the open one, and the Sallandse Heuvelrug rises east of them as dry heath on sand.
  • When: Late April to June by a distance. After mid-June the reeds close the view from most paths and roads. Swans and geese hold the open water in winter.
  • Getting there: Ossenzijl sits at the northern edge of Weerribben and its nature information centre is the usual starting point. Hogeweg runs south from the village for 5 km through the north-east of the reserve to the De Wicher windmill.
  • Look for: Purple Heron, Savi's Warbler, Bearded Reedling, Black Tern, Common Crane, Western Marsh Harrier, Black Grouse, European Nightjar
  • National parks: Weerribben-Wieden National Park, Sallandse Heuvelrug National Park
  • Stops:
    • De Weerribben : A national park of peat cuttings, reed and open water near Ossenzijl, with marked walks and canoe routes.
    • De Wieden : The lake and reedbed half of the same park, entered near Giethoorn. Purple Heron and Black Tern hunt over the water.
    • : A heath ridge national park near Nijverdal. A marked viewpoint looks over the last Dutch Black Grouse.
  • Also covers: Blokzijl, De Weerribben, De Wieden, Giethoorn, Holten, Nijverdal, Ossenzijl, Sallandse Heuvelrug National Park, Steenwijk, Weerribben-Wieden National Park
  • Also watch for: Otter was reintroduced to the Weerribben in 2002 and is now resident across the reserve, most often seen from a boat at first light. The Salland heath carries roe deer and adder, and the heather is at its best in August.

The IJsselmeer and the Afsluitdijk

Freshwater sea and dyke, one hour from Amsterdam

The Zuiderzee became a freshwater lake when the Afsluitdijk closed in 1932, and it is now the country's largest body of fresh water. Winter brings diving duck in numbers, and the dyke itself is a straight thirty two kilometre watchpoint.

  • Habitat: A 32 km dam between two bodies of water, salt on its northern side and fresh on its southern. Sluices at either end let the water through.
  • When: Worth a visit all year. Thousands of Scaup lie off the northern side of the dam in midwinter and Smew arrive in severe weather, and the sluice waters at Houtribsluizen are among the last to freeze. Warbler falls come down at Kornwerderzand in both spring and autumn.
  • Getting there: The motorway runs the length of the Afsluitdijk, with signed stopping places at Kornwerderzand near the Friesland end and at Breezanddijk halfway across. Houtribsluizen sits where the road reaches the coast between Lelystad and Enkhuizen.
  • Look for: Smew, Great Cormorant, Eurasian Wigeon, Common Tern
  • Parks and reserves: IJsselmeer (Natura 2000 site), Markermeer and IJmeer (Natura 2000 site)
  • Stops:
    • : The eastern end of the Afsluitdijk, where the outflow draws diving duck and gulls. There is parking and a walkway.
    • : The western sluices of the same dike, and a watchpoint for autumn passage.
    • Marker Wadden : A group of islands built for wildlife in the Markermeer, with hides and a lookout tower. A seasonal ferry runs from Lelystad.
  • Also covers: Den Oever sluices, Enkhuizen, IJsselmeer, Kornwerderzand, Makkum, Marker Wadden, Markermeer and IJmeer
  • Also watch for: The lake carries a large eel population and the fish passage at the Afsluitdijk was built for it. Harbour porpoise turn up on the seaward side of the dyke, most often in winter.

Flevoland and the Oostvaardersplassen

Reclaimed polder, reedbed and new islands, forty minutes from Amsterdam

Oostvaardersplassen grew on land drained in 1968 and became one of the most watched wetlands in Europe. White-tailed Eagle first bred here in 2006. Marker Wadden, the built archipelago a short boat ride north, adds bare sand and shell for terns and waders.

  • Habitat: A wetland of 72 square kilometres on land reclaimed from the Zuiderzee, holding open water, reedbed and wet grassland grazed by free-roaming cattle and horses, with forest plantations along the Knardijk on its landward side.
  • When: Good all year except when it freezes, and best through the breeding season and again in late summer from August to September. Light on the reserve from the Oostvaardersdijk is best in early morning and late afternoon.
  • Getting there: Leave the motorway at exit 10 for Lelystad and follow the road west. Torenvalkweg leaves it 1.5 km from the junction and runs 6 km to the Knardijk, and Buizerdweg leaves 3 km further on. Trains reach Lelystad from Amsterdam and Utrecht, and the Knardijk is 5 km due south of the station.
  • Look for: White-tailed Eagle, Great Egret, Eurasian Bittern, Bearded Reedling
  • Parks and reserves: Nieuw Land National Park, Veluwerandmeren (Natura 2000 site)
  • Stops:
    • : The two marked lookouts over the Oostvaardersplassen marsh, free and a short walk from the car parks.
    • Lepelaarplassen : Eurasian Spoonbill and heron ground on the Almere side, with a visitor centre and hides.
    • : The northeast corner of the polder. It is a migration watchpoint over open farmland.
  • Visitor centres: Bezoekerscentrum Oostvaardersplassen
  • Also covers: Bezoekerscentrum Oostvaardersplassen, De Kluut and Grote Praambult, Kamperhoek, Lelystad, Lepelaarplassen, Nieuw Land National Park, Veluwerandmeren, Zeewolde
  • Also watch for: Konik horses, red deer and Heck cattle graze the reserve as large herbivores, which is what keeps the reedbed and grassland in balance. The red deer rut runs through September and October.

The Veluwe

Heath, drift sand and pine and oak forest, one hour from Amsterdam

The largest area of continuous woodland and heath in the country, and the easiest place to work through the woodpeckers. Middle Spotted Woodpecker has spread here since the 1990s. Early mornings from April are when the forest is loudest.

  • Habitat: The largest continuous forest complex in north-western Europe, 50 km from Hattem in the north to Schaarsbergen in the south. Pine and oak woodland mix with open heath and drift sand, and Red Deer, Wild Boar, Mouflon and Pine Marten all hold ground here.
  • When: Spring and early summer for the forest birds. Honey Buzzard, Goshawk, Nightjar, Wryneck and Black Woodpecker are what birders come for, and Nightjar means staying until dusk.
  • Getting there: Motorways ring the Veluwe on all four sides and one crosses it from north to south. Apeldoorn sits at the northern intersection and Arnhem at the southern. Car access is increasingly restricted, and most of the Veluwe is explored by bicycle.
  • Look for: Middle Spotted Woodpecker, Black Woodpecker, Woodlark, Common Redstart
  • National parks: Hoge Veluwe National Park, Veluwezoom National Park
  • Stops:
    • Deelerwoud : Unfenced old woodland and heath between Arnhem and Apeldoorn, quiet and free to walk.
    • Planken Wambuis : Heath and drift sand, with marked walks from the car park on the Ede road. Woodlark and European Nightjar breed here.
    • De Hoge Veluwe : A national park with sit-in wildlife hides on the heath. It is the one park here that charges admission at the gate.
    • : The largest area of drift sand in western Europe. Walk in from the Kootwijk car park.
  • Also covers: De Hoge Veluwe, Deelerwoud, Hoenderloo, Hoge Veluwe National Park, Kootwijkerzand, Otterlo, Planken Wambuis, Veluwezoom National Park
  • Also watch for: Red deer, wild boar, roe deer and mouflon all live here, and the reserve runs marked wildlife viewing points for them. The red deer rut in September and October is the loudest time of the year.

The North Holland Dunes

Dune, scrub and dune lake, thirty minutes from Amsterdam

A continuous dune belt runs north from Haarlem, close enough to the city for a morning before a flight. Scrub and dune slack hold breeding warblers and Common Redstart, and the coast is a migration line for anything moving along the North Sea.

  • Habitat: A dune belt between Callantsoog and IJmuiden holding reedland and two large pools at Zwanenwater, brackish pits with muddy edges behind the Hondsbossche sea dike, and open dune grassland on the seaward side.
  • When: April to early July for the breeding birds at Zwanenwater. Camperduin turns on strong north-westerlies before 11 a.m. from August to October for shearwaters, Leach's Petrel, skuas and alcids, and spring passage there runs from late March to early June.
  • Getting there: The coastal Westerduinweg runs north from Petten to Callantsoog, and the Zwanenwater entrance is signed off it opposite the Uitlandweg junction. Camperduin and De Putten lie along the Hondsbossche Weg south of Petten. Buses from Schagen, Den Helder and Alkmaar serve the coast road.
  • Look for: Northern Wheatear, Common Redstart, European Stonechat, Eurasian Skylark
  • National park: Zuid-Kennemerland National Park
  • Stops:
    • : A long stone pier at the harbour mouth, walked out from the car park. A northwesterly gale brings the classic Dutch seabird passage.
    • Het Zwanenwater : Dune lakes north of Callantsoog with hides, for a small entry fee. A Eurasian Spoonbill colony nests here and Eurasian Bittern boom in the reed.
    • : A bird ringing station in the dunes, open to visitors on set mornings. You see migration in the hand.
    • : New dune and lagoon built on a rebuilt sea defence, with paths along the top.
  • Also covers: Camperduin and the Hondsbossche dunes, Castricum ringing station, Het Zwanenwater, Schoorl, The IJmuiden Zuidpier, Zuid-Kennemerland National Park
  • Also watch for: European bison graze the Kraansvlak enclosure at Zuid-Kennemerland, one of the few free-ranging herds in western Europe, alongside fallow deer and Konik horses. Rabbits keep the dune grassland short.

The South Holland Dunes

Dune, wooded valley and estate, forty minutes from Amsterdam

Meijendel and the Wassenaar estates hold older, wetter dune woodland than the north, which brings a different list within reach of The Hague. Terns pass offshore all summer, and the wooded parts are worth walking slowly in May.

  • Habitat: A dune belt running the North Sea coast from Katwijk south past Scheveningen, narrow along much of its length and backed by the Randstad cities, with wooded and canalised sections inland where water purification keeps pools ice-free through hard weather.
  • When: September and October, when the coast north of Katwijk aan Zee carries one of the heaviest landbird migrations in the country. The purification canals farther inland stay open in severe winters and hold Common Bittern, Smew, Goosander and Common Kingfisher at close range.
  • Getting there: Kwade Hoek sits southwest of the Haringvlietdam beside the marina harbour of Stellendam Buitenhaven. Snijderweg runs past the harbour, and a right turn opposite the Zuiderdiep pool reaches the high concrete coastal dike along the western edge of the harbour. A walk along the top of that dike gives a telescope view over the wide Kwade Hoek mudflats, which lie exposed at low tide.
  • Look for: Sandwich Tern, Common Hoopoe, Common Redstart, Icterine Warbler
  • National park: Hollandse Duinen National Park
  • Stops:
    • : Dune valleys and water channels behind Wassenaar, free and open, with a visitor centre and marked walks.
    • : Older, quieter dune between Katwijk and Wassenaar. Common Nightingale sing here in May.
    • Kwade Hoek : A sandy spit at the Haringvliet mouth, walked from the Ouddorp side. Terns and waders feed on it.
  • Also covers: Berkheide, Hollandse Duinen National Park, Kwade Hoek, Meijendel, Noordwijk, Wassenaar
  • Also watch for: Fallow deer and roe deer are common through Meijendel and the Wassenaar estates, and foxes hunt the dune slacks in daylight. The dune ponds hold a strong amphibian list in spring.

The Biesbosch and the Great Rivers

Tidal freshwater willow forest and river floodplain, one hour from Amsterdam

The Biesbosch is one of the last tidal freshwater wetlands in Europe, best seen from a boat among the willow. Water levels still rise and fall twice a day. East along the Rhine and Waal, reclaimed floodplain has brought herons and storks back to the river bends.

  • Habitat: A freshwater tidal marsh turned stable in 1970 when the Haringvlietdam closed, now carrying dense willow scrub and wet woodland cut by the Merwede and the Amer, with three large drinking water reservoirs at Petrusplaat, Honderd-en-Dertig and De Gijster.
  • When: Spring for the warblers, when 1,800 pairs of White-spotted Bluethroat sing from the scrub, and winter for the waterfowl roosting on the reservoirs with a White-tailed Eagle usually among them.
  • Getting there: There are no roads in the southern half of the Brabantse Biesbosch and it is entered by boat, rented at Drimmelen or Hank.
  • Look for: White-tailed Eagle, Purple Heron, Common Kingfisher, Great Egret
  • National park: De Biesbosch National Park
  • Stops:
    • Drimmelen boat routes : Quiet electric boats run into the creeks of the Biesbosch from Drimmelen. They are the only way to see the interior.
    • : Shallow water and willow scrub near Drimmelen, walked from the car park. A pair of White-tailed Eagle hold territory here.
    • : Tidal freshwater edge along the main channel. Bird it from the dike path.
    • : Floodplain further up the Waal, with wild grazing and marked walks, free and open.
  • Also covers: De Biesbosch National Park, De Millingerwaard, Drimmelen boat routes, Ooij, The Aakvlaai, The Nieuwe Merwede banks
  • Also watch for: Beaver was reintroduced here in 1988 and the lodges and gnawed willow are easy to find from a boat. Otter and roe deer both use the same creeks, and dusk is when the beavers move.

The Zeeland Delta

Tidal inlet, saltmarsh and shell bank, two hours from Amsterdam

The delta works left a chain of inlets, some tidal and some closed, each with its own birds. The Oosterschelde still fills and empties twice a day and holds waders through the winter. Bare shell banks carry the scarcest of the breeding plovers.

  • Habitat: Former sea inlets closed by the Delta dams. Grevelingen is now a 10,800 ha saltwater lake with no tide, and 3,000 ha of old tidal flat has dried out enough to hold nesting terns. The dune belt is narrow except at Westerschouwen, which is 3 km wide and well wooded.
  • When: All year, and the numbers make the case: up to 100,000 waterfowl and waders through the summer and close to 500,000 in winter. Sandwich Terns nest on the Grevelingen islets and a White-tailed Eagle often winters there.
  • Getting there: A road crosses the Brouwersdam between Goeree-Overflakkee and Schouwen-Duiveland and gives on to the Grevelingen shore at either end.
  • Look for: Kentish Plover, Pied Avocet, Eurasian Curlew, Dunlin, Barnacle Goose
  • National park: Oosterschelde National Park
  • Stops:
    • : Flooded fields inland from the Oosterschelde. You can see them from the road, and they are the best wader field in Zeeland.
    • : Dune and pine at the island tip near Burgh-Haamstede, with a migration watchpoint.
    • Yerseke Moer : Old salt marsh relief grazed by geese, with marked paths across it.
    • Waterdunen : A new tidal reserve at Breskens, free and open, with hides over the lagoon.
    • : The dam between Goeree and Schouwen. Scan from the pull-ins for divers, grebes and sea duck in winter.
  • Also covers: Domburg, Goes, Kop van Schouwen, Oosterschelde National Park, Prunje polder, Renesse, The Brouwersdam, Waterdunen, Yerseke Moer
  • Also watch for: Harbour and grey seals rest on the banks inside the Oosterschelde and are visible from the shore at low water. Harbour porpoise are regular in the tidal channels through the winter.

Limburg and the Southern Hills

Chalk grassland, hedgerow and beech wood, two hours from Amsterdam

The far south rises into chalk country that belongs more to the Ardennes than to the rest of the Netherlands. Hedged fields and beech wood hold birds found nowhere else in the country, and the walking is the only hill walking there is here.

  • Habitat: Humid heathland, woodland and fen at Meinweg in the south-east corner of the Netherlands, with deep flooded gravel pits either side of the Meuse north and south of Roermond that rarely freeze.
  • When: Late spring and early summer at Meinweg, and dusk for the twenty pairs of Nightjar. Winter for the Maasplassen gravel pits, which hold 30,000 waterfowl.
  • Getting there: From Roermond turn south-east towards Herkenbosch, and past the village turn left on the Grote Herkenbosserbaan, which runs more than 5 km north-east through Meinweg with parking areas and footpaths along it. The Elvenmeer pool at the far end is the Nightjar spot.
  • Look for: Red-backed Shrike, Middle Spotted Woodpecker, Common Redstart, Eurasian Skylark
  • National parks: De Maasduinen National Park, De Groote Peel National Park, Meinweg National Park
  • Stops:
    • De Groote Peel : A national park of raised bog on the Brabant border, with marked walks. Common Crane roost here in autumn.
    • De Meinweg : A national park of heath and terrace woodland on the German border. European Nightjar churr at dusk and adders lie on the paths.
    • : Stream valleys in the south hills, with public footpaths through old oak. Middle Spotted Woodpecker hold territory in it.
    • : A former marl quarry, now open as a nature area. Eurasian Eagle-Owl nest on its faces.
  • Also covers: Bergen (Limburg), De Groote Peel National Park, De Maasduinen National Park, De Meinweg, Epen, Meinweg National Park, The ENCI quarry, Maastricht, The Gulp and Geul valleys, Valkenburg, Well (Limburg)
  • Also watch for: Badger and roe deer work the hedged fields, and wildcat has returned to the woods along the Belgian and German border. Fire salamanders emerge on wet nights from April to October.

Preparation

BeakBrain Learn the Dutch list before you travel 539 species as collector cards, with short daily rounds that teach them by sight and sound. Learn these 542 birds before you fly

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the best time to go birding in the Netherlands?

April and May for breeding birds and full song, September and October for wader passage through the Wadden Sea, and December to February for geese in six figures.

Do I need a car?

No, and the Netherlands is one of the few countries where that is genuinely true. Every region above is reachable by train, and OV-fiets rents a bike at over 300 stations for EUR 4.80 a day, which is how most Dutch birders get from the platform to the reserve. 9292 plans train, bus and ferry together, and the island ferries connect to island buses. A car is still faster if you want to work several sites in one morning, or reach the quieter parts of the Veluwe, Drenthe and Zeeland, where buses are thin outside peak hours. Many island and dune properties lend or rent bikes, which is worth asking when you book.

How much does a birding trip here cost?

Accommodation is the largest line. Rate bands above run from about $100 a night in the mid range to $500 and above at the top, and winter is consistently the cheapest season.

Do I need to book the island ferries?

As a foot passenger, no. With a car in summer or at a weekend, yes, and well ahead for Texel. Three operators run the five islands: TESO to Texel, Rederij Doeksen to Vlieland and Terschelling, and Wagenborg to Ameland and Schiermonnikoog. Schiermonnikoog is car free for visitors, so you park on the mainland at Lauwersoog whatever you arrive in.

Are the reserves free to enter?

Most are open and free to walk, and that includes the national parks and the Natura 2000 sites the regions above are built around. Some hides and boat trips are ticketed, a few breeding areas are closed in season, which is marked on the ground, and De Hoge Veluwe is the one park here that charges admission at the gate.

Is autumn seabird passage worth a day?

On the right day it is the best birding in the country. A northwesterly gale in October pushes seabirds close inshore and the piers turn into grandstands: Northern Gannet and Black-legged Kittiwake in numbers, Great Skua and Pomarine Jaeger chasing terns, Sooty Shearwater and Northern Fulmar passing offshore, and Little Gull and Common Scoter moving in streams. The Zuidpier at IJmuiden in The North Holland Dunes is the classic stand, with Camperduin further north and the Brouwersdam in The Zeeland Delta covering the southwest.

Wind decides everything. A westerly or northwesterly force six and above puts birds within range, and a calm day off the same pier is quiet, so watch the forecast rather than the calendar. Counts posted on Trektellen tell you what moved past each station that morning, which is the fastest way to know whether it is worth the drive. Dress for standing still in cold spray, and this is the one Dutch birding day where a scope on a solid tripod is doing all the work.

Is it worth going out at night?

For four birds, yes. European Nightjar churrs over the heath from late May into July, on the The Veluwe sands and the Drenthe heaths in Groningen and Drenthe, and the half hour after sunset is the whole show. Eurasian Bittern booms from the reedbeds at dusk in The Weerribben-Wieden and the Salland Ridge and Flevoland and the Oostvaardersplassen from March. Tawny Owl calls through the wooded estates from January, Long-eared Owl gathers in winter roosts that local clubs know the location of, and Eurasian Woodcock roding over the woods at dusk in spring is a Veluwe speciality.

Many Dutch reserves close at sunset and the rule is posted at the entrance, so the practical approach is to stand on a public track or a dike at the edge and let the sound come to you. The clubs listed in the community section run evening excursions in nightjar season and they know which heath is holding birds this year.

What should I bring?

A telescope, if you can borrow or afford one. Dutch birding is tidal flats, goose fields and open water, and much of what you are looking at sits a long way off, so a scope on a tripod turns a distant grey smudge into a bird. Binoculars are the thing you actually need though, and 8x42 is the usual all-round choice. Then dress for wind: there is nothing between the North Sea and you, so layers and a waterproof shell work better than one thick coat, and gloves are welcome from October.

The field guide most Dutch birders carry is the Collins Bird Guide, by Svensson, Mullarney and Zetterstrom, sold here as the ANWB Vogelgids van Europa. Vogelbescherming keeps free identification material online in Dutch and English. Walking boots are enough for the dikes and dune paths, and wellingtons are worth having if you plan on the meadow reserves after rain.

How does the tide affect a Wadden Sea visit?

It decides the day. Birds feed spread out across the flats at low water and gather on roosts as the tide covers them, so the hour before and after high water is when you see numbers in one place. Check the table for the station nearest your hide on Rijkswaterstaat Waterinfo, which is the official Dutch tide service.

Can I bird here with limited mobility?

Often yes, and it varies by site. A good deal of the birding here happens from roadsides, hides and lodge grounds rather than on long walks, and some reserves keep flat, surfaced trails. Ask a lodge or reserve directly about step free access, surfaces and seating before you book. The Birdability Map records those details for birding sites, and their Access Considerations guide lists the questions worth asking. Coverage is thin outside the United States, so read a blank area as unrecorded rather than unsuitable.

Birding Community

Alongside the national bodies below, the Netherlands has 26 local bird clubs across 12 regions. See every Dutch club by region.

Vogelbescherming Nederland BirdLife in the Netherlands, with reserve information and identification guides in Dutch and English. Visit Sovon Vogelonderzoek Nederland The national bird monitoring organisation, and the source behind most Dutch population figures.
